title: Explainable Geospatial AI Reveals Associations Between Ambient Air Quality and Thermal Predictors of Child Respiratory Disease in Bangladesh
content:
Abstract

Air pollution poses a substantial threat to child health, yet evidence on the spatial relationship between fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and acute respiratory infection (ARI) at the upazila (sub-district) level remains limited in Bangladesh. This study integrated 1-km MAIAC-derived PM2.5, land surface temperature (LST), and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) with 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey data (8,784 children under five, 344 upazilas), assigning exposures via a buffer-based approach to account for survey-cluster displacement. An explainable machine learning framework combining Random Forest and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) predicted ARI and quantified how temperature, vegetation, and PM2.5 jointly contribute to spatial variation in risk. PM2.5 ranged from 34.8 to 92.7 μg/m3, exceeding the World Health Organization annual guideline by roughly 7–18-fold, with the highest levels in northwestern Bangladesh; ARI prevalence was 1.08% (n = 95). The model achieved moderate predictive performance (standard cross-validation AUC–ROC = 0.667; spatial cross-validation AUC–ROC = 0.544). Environmental variables were the primary predictors, with LST (0.328), NDVI (0.293), and PM2.5 (0.279) together accounting for approximately 90% of feature importance. PM2.5 ranked third in both importance measures. SHAP analysis revealed a nonlinear exposure–response association, with an exploratory PM2.5 inflection region of approximately 55–65 μg/m3 above which ARI risk rose more rapidly, while greater vegetation cover showed a protective association. Northwestern upazilas emerged as priority areas. These findings suggest explainable geospatial AI can identify multi-environmental spatial risk patterns in childhood respiratory health, offering a practical framework for spatial prioritization (not PM2.5-specific burden estimation) and public health planning in data-constrained settings.
author: Md Moniruzzaman
